CausalChain: Radiotherapy → releases tumor neoantigens → activates local T cell response in TIME → peripheral STIE is still suppressed by tumor-derived factors (e.g., artemin from Ter cells) → persistent artemin prevents clonal replacement of exhausted T cells (characterized by low TCF1) → leads to reduced antitumor immunity and potential hyperprogression → artemin inhibition may relieve systemic immune suppression → enhances proliferation of precursor exhausted T cells and improves efficacy of Pd-1 blockade
Hypothesis: Tumor-derived artemin secreted by Ter cells sustains an immunosuppressive systemic immune environment that impairs the clonal replacement of exhausted T cells and limits the efficacy of Pd-1 blockade; therefore, combining radiotherapy with targeted artemin inhibition will reprogram both the STIE and TIME to boost the expansion of functional T cell clones and improve clinical outcomes in patients treated with immunotherapy.
Abstract: Tumor immunotherapy outcomes are influenced not only by the local tumor immune microenvironment (TIME) but also by systemic immune regulators present in the systemic tumor immune environment (STIE). Radiotherapy is known to stimulate immunogenic cell death and reprogram the TIME, while systemic factors released by tumor‐associated cells (for example, Ter cells that secrete artemin) may impair the proliferation and effectiveness of T cell populations. Here, we propose that tumor‐derived artemin maintains an immunosuppressive milieu in the STIE by preventing the clonal replacement of exhausted T cell subsets. Accordingly, the combination of radiotherapy with targeted inhibition of artemin signaling could reprogram both STIE and TIME, thereby enhancing the expansion of precursor exhausted T cells and improving the efficacy of anti–Pd‐1 therapy. This strategy may be particularly relevant in patient subsets that exhibit hyperprogressive disease following Pd‐1 inhibitor monotherapy.
